Distribution functions for Yes/No SDT

Source: R/distributions.R
sdt_yn_dist.Rd

Density and random generation for the yes/no signal detection theory model, where the response is the number of "old"/"signal" responses out of a fixed number of trials (a binomial likelihood).

Usage

dsdt_yn(
  n_old,
  n_trials,
  stimulus,
  d,
  criterion = NULL,
  bias = NULL,
  sdratio = 1,
  dist = c("normal", "gumbel_min", "gumbel_max", "logistic"),
  log = FALSE
)

rsdt_yn(
  n,
  n_trials,
  stimulus,
  d,
  criterion = NULL,
  bias = NULL,
  sdratio = 1,
  dist = c("normal", "gumbel_min", "gumbel_max", "logistic")
)

Arguments

n_old

Integer vector. Number of "old"/"signal" responses.

n_trials

Integer vector. Total number of trials per cell.

stimulus

Numeric or logical vector (0/1). Stimulus type: 0 = noise, 1 = signal.

d

Numeric. Sensitivity: \(d'\) when sdratio is 1, and otherwise the balanced index \(d_a\), the separation between the two distributions divided by the root-mean-square of their SDs (see sdt_yn()). The separation in noise units is d * sqrt((1 + sdratio^2) / 2).

criterion

Numeric. Location of the decision criterion, measured from the mean of the noise distribution in units of its SD. Give either criterion or bias, not both.

bias

Numeric. Location of the decision criterion measured from the midpoint between the noise and signal means instead, in noise-SD units: criterion - d * sqrt((1 + sdratio^2) / 2) / 2. 0 is the neutral point, positive values a bias toward "new"/"noise".

sdratio

Numeric. Ratio of signal to noise standard deviations (default 1, i.e., equal variance). Must be positive, and is on the natural scale — see the section below before reusing a fitted value.

dist

Character. The distribution assumed for the latent evidence, given here by its cumulative distribution function:

  • "normal" (default): Gaussian, \(\Phi(x)\)

  • "gumbel_min": smallest extreme value, \(1 - \exp(-\exp(x))\) (the complementary log-log distribution)

  • "gumbel_max": largest extreme value, \(\exp(-\exp(-x))\) (the log-log distribution, as in evd::pgumbel)

  • "logistic": \(1 / (1 + \exp(-x))\)

log

Logical. If TRUE, returns log-density (default FALSE).

n

Integer. Number of observations to generate. n_trials, stimulus, and the model parameters are recycled to this length.

Value

dsdt_yn returns the (log-)density (binomial probability). rsdt_yn returns an integer vector with the number of "old"/"signal" responses per observation.

Parameter scales

As everywhere in bmm, these functions take their arguments on the natural scale, while the parameters sdt_yn() estimates are on their link scale. d and criterion have identity links and carry across unchanged, but sdratio has a log link: a fitted sdratio of 0.375 is a ratio of exp(0.375) = 1.455, and passing 0.375 here instead asks for a signal distribution 2.7 times narrower than the noise. That is a legal value and raises no error, so exponentiate first.

Vector arguments

  • r*(n, ...) returns exactly n draws: a vector, or a data frame or matrix with n rows. Every per-observation argument (a parameter, a stimulus, a number of trials) is recycled to length n with rep_len(), as in stats::rnorm(): draw i uses element i, and a matrix is read element by element; only a set of values per draw, such as thresholds, takes row i of a matrix (see below). A shorter vector is repeated, also when n is not a multiple of its length. Until bmm 1.6.0 at the earliest, rddm() with n = 1 and parameter vectors still returns one draw per element, with a deprecation warning.

  • n is a single number of at least 0. A fraction is truncated, as in stats::rnorm(), and n = 0 gives an empty vector, or a matrix or data frame with zero rows and the usual columns. Unlike stats::rnorm(), which takes the length of a vector n, these functions stop on one; rddm() still takes its length, with a deprecation warning.

  • d*(x, ...) returns one value per observation: as many as the longest of x (its rows, when the observations are rows of counts) and the per-observation arguments, the others recycled to that length. Value i is what the call on the i-th elements alone returns. A matrix in an argument that takes one number per observation, such as x or d, holds one observation per element, as in stats::dnorm(). When x or any per-observation argument is empty, the result is empty, as in stats::dnorm(). A NULL argument, such as a misspelt column of a data frame, counts as empty, except where the default is NULL, as for criterion or kcrit: there it means that the argument is not given. Where an observation is a vector of counts (dsdt_rating(), dsdt_dpsdt(), dsdt_metad(), dsdt_ranking() and dsdt_cdp()), or the pair of mean_rt or var_rt values of dezdm(version = "4par"), a vector is always one observation: pass a matrix with zero rows for none, as an empty vector stops. An empty kcrit of dsdt_cdp() and rsdt_cdp() stops as well; kcrit = NULL gives the R/K model. Counts in a data frame, a tibble included, are read as the matrix of its rows, and so are mean_rt and var_rt of dezdm(version = "4par"). dsdm() with a data frame x is the exception: it returns a data frame of the same shape, one density per cell, and cuts longer parameters to the number of cells.

  • A set of values that describes one observation, such as the thresholds of the rating models, is a vector when every observation shares it and a matrix with one row per observation otherwise: row i belongs to observation i, or to draw i.

  • Configuration arguments such as version, dist, log, parametrization and n_new are single values and are never recycled. An argument that a version does not use, such as zr of dezdm(version = "3par"), is ignored.

References

Green, D. M., & Swets, J. A. (1966). Signal detection theory and psychophysics. Wiley.

Examples

# Density of yes/no SDT data
dsdt_yn(n_old = 80, n_trials = 100, stimulus = 1,
        d = 1.5, criterion = 0.9)
#> [1] 0.02264629

# The same observer, with the criterion given relative to the midpoint
dsdt_yn(n_old = 80, n_trials = 100, stimulus = 1,
        d = 1.5, bias = 0.15)
#> [1] 0.02264629

# Vectorized over observations
dsdt_yn(n_old = c(30, 80), n_trials = c(100, 100),
        stimulus = c(0, 1), d = 1.5, criterion = 0.9,
        log = TRUE)
#> [1] -6.371711 -3.787759

# Unequal variance from a fitted model: sdt_yn() reports sdratio on its log
# link, so exponentiate before passing it here
dsdt_yn(n_old = 80, n_trials = 100, stimulus = 1,
        d = 1.5, criterion = 0.9, sdratio = exp(0.375))
#> [1] 0.04679876
# Generate yes/no SDT data for a design
dat <- expand.grid(id = 1:20, stimulus = c(0L, 1L))
dat$n_trials <- 100L
dat$n_old <- rsdt_yn(nrow(dat), dat$n_trials, dat$stimulus,
                     d = 1.5, criterion = 0.9)
head(dat)
#>   id stimulus n_trials n_old
#> 1  1        0      100    22
#> 2  2        0      100    16
#> 3  3        0      100    19
#> 4  4        0      100    16
#> 5  5        0      100    21
#> 6  6        0      100    18
